title: Cruelty as a divorce ground - what courts actually accept as evidence
p1:
Can a marriage end because of repeated insults, humiliation or emotional abuse?

Yes. But there is a legal distinction many people overlook: not every disagreement, argument or unpleasant incident amounts to cruelty in the eyes of a court.
p2:
Under Indian matrimonial law, cruelty can be physical or mental. And mental cruelty does not necessarily leave visible injuries.

Courts examine the overall pattern of behaviour, its seriousness, its frequency and its impact on the marital relationship.

What can help establish cruelty? Medical records, messages, emails, call recordings where legally admissible, witness testimony, police complaints and documented incidents may all become relevant evidence.

One surprising point: a single incident is not automatically insufficient. Depending on its gravity and circumstances, even one exceptionally serious act may amount to cruelty.
p3:
Here is the practical distinction: making an allegation is not the same as proving it.

Courts look beyond emotional accusations and examine whether the conduct, viewed objectively and in its complete context, makes it unreasonable to expect the spouse to continue the marriage.

A consistent record of incidents, supported by credible evidence, can be far more persuasive than exaggerated claims or isolated statements.

The real question is not simply whether a marriage was unhappy, but whether the conduct crossed the legal threshold of cruelty.
conclusion: Should repeated emotional humiliation be treated as seriously as physical violence when courts decide whether cruelty has occurred? What do you think?
